newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firms at Euro close, buoyed by short-covering.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firms at Euro close, buoyed by short-covering.

text.p: The dollar closed firmer in Europe, shrugging off earlier weakness amid short-covering and finding some solace in U.S. data showing robust economic growth and signs of a tight labour market, dealers said.
The market's listless end-of-month mood limited gains though as dealers awaited Friday's U.S. jobs data for July for a clearer picture of labour market strenght.

"The dollar is still looking punchy," said David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel in London. "It is quite simply in a win-win situation, and downmoves are merely a correction rather than a change in trend."
The U.S. economy expanded at a rate of 2.2 percent in the second quarter, above expectations for a 1.9 percent increase.
However, first quarter growth was revised down sustantially to 4.9 percent from its originally reported 5.9 percent.

Weekly labour market data showed a marked fall in jobless claims from 299,000 to 277,000, its lowest level since January 1974. The Labor Department attributed the drop to distortions from seasonal factors.
Dollar/yen was at the mercy of mixed messages out of Japan, regaining ground above 118 yen in European trading after easing below the figure overnight.
Comments from a Japanese auto industry official sparked fears U.S.- Japan trade tensions could resurface.

Takao Tominaga, vice-chairman of Japan's Automobile Manufacturers' Association, pegged the appropriate range for dollar/yen between 110 and 120 yen, and said he did not want the rate to strengthen from its current levels due to its implications for trade.

But after the dollar eased to a low of 117.48 traders scurried to cover shorts, pushing dollar/yen to a high of 118.15. At 1500 GMT it was at 118.38/48, compared with 118.15/25 in late European trading on Wednesday.

The trade comments came soon after remarks from U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshevsky, who said earlier this week that Japan had not gone far enough in opening up its auto market to outside competition.

But the dollar made a comeback after comments from an ex-ministry of finance official - saying that Japan or the U.S. would not need to take action if the dollar rose above 120 yen and that it did not need to raise its official discount rate for some time as prices were stable.
Non-farm payrolls are expected to grow by 193,000 in July after a rise of 217,000 in June.
Even though jobs data are still a key indicator, traders said the market was more focused on wage costs.

On Tuesday, the second quarter employment cost index showed a rise of 0.8 percent after a 0.6 percent increase in the previous three months. However, employers granted wage and salary increases at a rate of 0.8 percent, compared to 0.9 percent in the first quarter.
"You would have to get figures way out of line with market expectations to change the scenario," said a senior trader at a German bank. "And the dollar will take it in it's stride either way."

Elsewhere in Europe, the guilder was steady afer the Dutch central bank said it bought guilders for marks on Wednesday, and after it kept key money market rate unchanged at 3.00 percent.

There had been talk of a possible Dutch rate rise as the guilder fell to 47-month lows on Tuesday, to below its ERM midpoint of 1.12673 per mark. The guilder was at 1.126300/6350 versus late Wednesday's 1.126250/6350.

Sterling recaptured ground above 3.00 marks, aided by UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's coments. He said in a newspaper interview that he had no plans for a special autumn budget to attempt to brake consumer spending and also hinted at no intervention to stem the pound's gains.
Sterling/mark was at 3.0130/40 versus 2.9890/00 at the previous European close.-- A. London newsroom + 44 171 5427792
